abstract:
Researchers identified a role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease, with the result of brain tissue analyses and experiments in mice indicating that galectin-3 acts as a modulator of Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and microglial responses.

The post Alzheimer’s Study Shows Gal3 Shapes Aβ Remodeling and Microglial Responses appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Sophia Ktori

content.value:
Researchers at Lund University in Sweden, in collaboration with teams at University of Seville and at the Instituto de Biomedicina de Sevilla (IBiS), have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 (Gal3) in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The researchers’ study, involving analysis of postmortem human brain tissue, cell-based lab studies, and experiments in mice, found that galectin-3 influences how the brain’s immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease’s characteristic amyloid plaques. The results also indicated that galectin-3 is involved in shaping the plaques themselves and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

“This discovery provides new insights into the mechanisms of the disease and identifies galectin-3 as a potential future therapeutic target”, said Lluís Camprubí-Ferrer, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at Lund University. Camprubí-Ferrer is co-first author of the researchers’ published paper in PNAS, titled “Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregationand lysosomal processing,” in which they conclude that their collective findings “identify Gal3 as a modulator of Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and microglial responses in AD.”

Alzheimer’s disease is characterized by accumulations of beta-amyloid (Aβ) in the brain. These proteins clump together to form plaques. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, play “central roles” in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, the authors noted. Microglia mediate neuroinflammation in response to specific stimuli through a range of receptors and signalling pathways. “One such stimulus is amyloid-beta (Aβ), a highly aggregation-prone peptide that accumulates in the form of plaques in Alzheimer’s disease (AD),” the team continued. However, they noted, while neuroinflammation and amyloid-β pathology are central features of Alzheimer’s disease,  “… the mechanisms linking amyloid pathology to microglial dysfunction remain incompletely understood.”

In a previous study the research team at Lund University showed for the first time that the protein galectin-3 increases in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease, and that removing the protein decreased inflammation in the brain. “Our group and others have shown that Gal3 is upregulated in microglia surrounding Aβ plaques and that its deletion reduces plaque burden and inflammation in mouse models,” they stated, noting that prior research has also identified Gal3 as “one of the top five upregulated proteins in AD brain.”

Through their newly reported study the researchers have shown the direct relationship between galectin-3 and Aβ plaques, with data from animal studies showing a cause-and-effect relationships, and human tissue analyses demonstrating a strong correlation.

The results showed that galectin-3 binds to Aβ, and that it also acts within the lysosomes. Outside the microglia galectin-3 sits on the plaque itself, where it changes the shape of the amyloid fibers as they grow. “No one has previously shown what galectin-3 does to the plaque itself,” explained Camprubí-Ferrer. “We have observed that the protein binds to long protein strands known as amyloid fibrils, blocking one of the steps by which they multiply and altering their shape. In cell experiments, the fibrils reshaped by galectin-3 went on to damage nerve cells.” Galectin-3, the researchers concluded, is not merely present around the plaque, it actively shapes it.

The research also showed that inside the microglia galectin-3 sits in the lysosomes (the compartments in which the cell breaks down waste, worn out components and macromolecules), where it steers how amyloid is processed.

When the researchers then removed galectin-3 in mice with an Alzheimer’s-like disease, the plaques became smaller and more tightly packed. The surrounding nerve endings were damaged to a significantly lesser extent, and the microglia shifted from an aggressive, inflammatory state to a protective one. “In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency alters plaque architecture, reduces plaque-associated neuritic pathology, and increases TREM2 coverage,” the scientists reported.

“When we inactivated galectin-3, microglia transitioned from their harmful state to a state rich in the protective receptor TREM2, a protein that we know plays an important role in the brain’s immune defence and in the risk of Alzheimer’s disease”, added Camprubí-Ferrer. The collective results, they stated, “…  position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated micro-glial responses in AD.”

The results of the animal studies are clear-cut, showing a cause-and-effect relationship. The experiments on human tissue, from nine individuals, show a strong correlation. What the researchers cannot yet say is whether blocking galectin-3 helps patients.

“This is important because current Alzheimer’s drugs target amyloid without helping to reduce inflammation in the brain. And galectin-3 is a protein that drugs can actually bind to,” said Camprubí-Ferrer.

“And the timing is right,” added Tomas Deierborg, PhD, professor and leader of the Experimental Neuroinflammation research group at Lund University. “Drugs containing antibodies that break down amyloid have reached patients, but their modest effect has drawn attention to the brain’s immune response. That is where we can now fill in the gaps.”

Deierborg finds it particularly encouraging that their early discoveries have now led to clinical trials. “From a therapeutic perspective, these findings support further investigation of Gal3 modulation in AD, particularly in light of ongoing efforts to develop Gal3-targeting monoclonal antibodies [Phase Ib/IIa, NCT05074498] and BBB-permeable small-molecule inhibitors,” Deierbor stated. Within the last few weeks U.S. regulators gave the go-ahead for a Phase II trial of an antibody that blocks galectin-3. “This demonstrates the clinical potential of our research findings,” Deierborg stated.
